title: Finite-temperature phase diagram of dipolar bosons in a cylindrical setup
authors: Juan Sánchez-Baena, Raúl Bombín, Jordi Boronat
abstract: Temperature plays a non-trivial role in dipolar systems, being able to either induce or destroy spatial density modulations. In order to shed light into the interplay between thermal effects and quantum correlations, we employ the path integral Monte Carlo method (PIMC) to obtain the phase diagram of a system of dipolar bosons in an infinite cylindrical geometry and at finite temperatures. For a fixed total density, we vary the scattering length of the interaction and the temperature, and characterize the structure and superfluidity of the emerging phases. The PIMC method accounts for thermal effects and quantum correlations at all orders, and can be used to quantitatively estimate the superfluid fraction of the system. Remarkably, we find a regime of parameters where, starting from a supersolid, the spatial order vanishes with temperature before the superfluidity does. We also find a region of the phase diagram where the superfluid fraction displays a non-monotonous dependence with temperature. Our results extend previous descriptions, relying on Bogoliubov theory, to larger temperatures in the thermodynamic limit and illustrate how spatial modulations and superfluidity are lost as temperature is increased.
summary: This work uses Path Integral Monte Carlo simulations to map the finite-temperature phase diagram of dipolar bosons in a cylinder. It reveals novel physics, such as the decoupling of spatial order loss from superfluidity loss, and demonstrates non-monotonic temperature dependence in superfluidity. These findings significantly extend theoretical understanding of quantum correlations in dipolar quantum gases.
main_problem: To investigate the complex interplay between thermal effects and quantum correlations in dipolar bosonic systems by mapping out the finite-temperature phase diagram.
main_result: The study reveals a regime where spatial order vanishes before superfluidity, and demonstrates a non-monotonic dependence of the superfluid fraction on temperature.
method: The Path Integral Monte Carlo (PIMC) method is employed to calculate thermodynamic properties, supplemented by Extended Gross-Pitaevskii simulations (eGPE) for comparison.
model_or_system: The system consists of dipolar bosons confined within an infinite cylindrical geometry. The interaction potential includes long-range dipolar terms, modeled by a Hamiltonian incorporating kinetic and dipolar interaction energy terms.
key_observables: Superfluid fraction ($ho_s/ho$), structural contrast of the x-column density ($C$), and the full phase diagram mapping.
important_parameters: Temperature ($T$) relative to the critical temperature ($T_c$), scattering length ($a$), and the fixed mean density ($ho_{	ext{mean}}$).
main_assumptions: The PIMC method uses the fourth-order Chin's action, and the study uses an approximation of a fixed box size ($L_x = 40r_0$) due to computational constraints.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate representative snapshots of supersolid and superfluid phases, and plot the structural contrast and superfluid fraction as functions of scattering length for various temperatures.
paper_structure: The paper systematically maps the phase diagram by varying temperature and scattering length, defining phases (Solid, Supersolid, Superfluid, Normal) using criteria based on structural contrast ($C$) and superfluid fraction ($f_s$).
why_interesting: It provides quantitative, high-temperature results for dipolar quantum fluids, extending beyond mean-field theories and elucidating the relative thermal stability of spatial order versus superfluidity.
